```{r setup}
library(risikoR)
```

Risk looks like a game of luck. It is, but the luck is completely
characterised: every roll of the dice has an exact distribution, every battle
is an absorbing Markov chain, and both can be written down. This article walks
from one throw of the dice up to whole-game win rates.

## One throw of the dice

There are `6^n_att * 6^n_def` equally likely combinations, few enough to
enumerate exhaustively. `rk_duel_dist()` does exactly that.

```{r}
rk_duel_dist(3, 2)
```

Three attacking dice against two defending dice is the standard case, and it
is worth memorising: the attacker loses nothing about 37% of the time, trades
one for one about 34% of the time, and loses two about 29% of the time.

Comparing every legal dice pairing shows how much the extra dice are worth:

```{r}
pairings <- expand.grid(n_att = 1:3, n_def = 1:2)
odds <- do.call(
  rbind,
  Map(rk_duel_odds, pairings$n_att, pairings$n_def)
)
odds[order(odds$n_def, odds$n_att), ]
```

Two lessons fall out. Rolling three dice instead of one roughly halves the
attacker's expected loss, so never attack with fewer armies than you need for
three dice. And the defender's second die is worth more than the attacker's
third: with two defending dice the attacker loses more armies than the
defender in every pairing.

## The whole battle

A battle repeats the duel until one side runs out. Because each duel removes a
fixed number of armies, the process is an absorbing Markov chain over states
`(attacker armies, defender armies)` — which `rk_battle_odds(method = "exact")`
solves directly.

```{r}
rk_battle_odds(10, 8, method = "exact")
```

The Monte Carlo estimate converges to it:

```{r}
set.seed(1)
mc <- do.call(rbind, lapply(
  c(100, 1000, 10000),
  function(n) rk_battle_odds(10, 8, n = n)
))
mc$exact <- rk_battle_odds(10, 8, method = "exact")$p_conquer
mc[, c("n", "p_conquer", "exact")]
```

Holding the attacker fixed and varying the defender traces the conquest curve:

```{r}
rk_plot_conquest(20, def_range = 1:25, method = "exact")
```

The crossing point is the number to remember: an attacker needs roughly a
**5-to-4 advantage** for even odds, and about a 3-to-2 advantage to be
comfortable.

```{r}
odds_grid <- rk_odds_table(att_range = 2:20, def_range = 1:20)
even <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(odds_grid, odds_grid$def_armies), function(d) {
  win <- d[d$p_conquer >= 0.5, ]
  if (nrow(win) == 0) return(NULL)
  win[1, c("def_armies", "att_armies", "p_conquer")]
}))
head(even, 10)
```

The whole surface at once:

```{r, fig.height = 5}
rk_plot_odds_heatmap(att_range = 2:20, def_range = 1:20)
```

## From battles to games

Exact odds do not settle the game, because a game is a sequence of decisions
about *which* battles to fight. The built-in agents encode three answers:

* `"random"` attacks at random,
* `"aggressive"` attacks the weakest reachable enemy while it outnumbers them,
* `"cautious"` attacks only above an army ratio and otherwise consolidates.

`rk_tournament()` deals a fresh board for every game and plays it out.

```{r}
results <- rk_tournament(
  c(Red = "aggressive", Blue = "cautious", Green = "random"),
  n_games = 12,
  max_rounds = 40,
  seed = 1
)
results
```

```{r}
rk_plot_tournament(results)
```

Win rates depend on the round cap: aggression is rewarded when games are cut
short, patience when they are allowed to run.

```{r}
caps <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c(10, 40), function(cap) {
  out <- rk_tournament(
    c(Red = "aggressive", Blue = "cautious"),
    n_games = 8, max_rounds = cap, seed = 2
  )
  out$max_rounds <- cap
  out
}))
caps[, c("max_rounds", "player", "strategy", "win_rate", "mean_rounds")]
```

## Where the model stops

The engine implements the combat rules exactly, but a full game of Risk also
has cards, sets traded for armies, and the rule that a conquering player draws
a card. Those are not modelled here, so tournament win rates describe *these*
agents on *this* board rather than the printed game in full.
